root_tweet.text: A democratic system survives only if its shared information system isn't polluted with disinformation. A democratic system cannot survive if lying is endemic.

children.text: For democracies to survive in a world of exponential complexity growth, the decision-making (i.e. how the sausage is made) must be more transparent. Democracy is more robust than alternatives due to its error-correcting foundation.

Democracy is not only an egalitarian game where everyone can vote, it also must be a transparent game.  It's a controlled conflict where the victor rises to the top of governance by conforming to norms and not violating rules. https://t.co/XExEwwpT9o

What can be missing in representational democracies (i.e. people represent the will of subsets of the citizens) is that the decision-making process of governance is not required to be transparent.  This is problematic for complex problems like a pandemic response.

Propaganda is a way to keep hidden the decision-making process. The free press is the mechanism to make public the decision-making process. Democracies themselves are not required to reveal their own decision-making process. Information is encapsulated within the governing body.

Direct representational systems however function with decision-making being transparent all the time.  But because of the lack of information encapsulation, it becomes unwieldy and leads to information overload. What is needed are decision-making processes that scale.

Our present-day governance institutions have not kept up with technology.  Governments refuse to adopt new rules because its own players are too comfortable gaming the status quo.  Goodhart's Law runs wild in government.

Civilization had to discover a new world (i.e. Americas) to invent new governance rules (i.e. Democracy). Unfortunately, humanity has no new worlds to discover and is thus unable to re-invent new governance processes.

We are essentially held in prison by our existing medieval governance institutions. Humanity is unable to rise to the challenge of growing technology complexity because we have antiquated processes that are constantly being gamed for the benefit of the very few.

New worlds of abundance like the Americas don't exist.  Mars is a world of scarcity and most likely will only lead towards a martial culture and governance. The key ingredient for democracy to prosper is abundance.  But unfortunately there are no new worlds of abundance.

Aside from reaching the limits of medieval governance, we are reaching the earth's ecological limits. Our technologies can't progress fast enough to address either of these limitations. We are thus heading for a collapse. But what kind of a collapse will this look like?

The problem with many scenarios of how civilization collapses is that it myopically employs history as a guide. The problem with history is that the past does not mirror the conditions of the present.  That's because the present has technology that did not exist in the past.

Russia's invasion is an instructive example of societal conflict.  Surprisingly the internet infrastructure, electricity, water, and the food supply remain operational. The global pandemic also surprisingly did not cause an infrastructure catastrophe.

There were supply chain disruptions, but nothing dramatic for almost every country in the world.  People went on with their daily lives despite a raging virus. The poorest of nations coped just as well as the richest of nations.

Most nations today are driven by market economies and despite poverty can be robust enough to maintain the local population. Civilization collapse will unlikely lead to the anarchic Mad Max scenario that Western preppers plan their entire lives around.

Civilization collapse more likely will look like Elysium.  That is where there is a pronounced difference between the haves and the have-nots. If you live in the have-not world, then it'll look like any failed state.

So it's no surprise that there is a penchant for prepping in rural America. That's because rural America sees the writing on the wall. Furthermore, they've bought into the narrative that cities will look more like 'Escape from NY' without realizing that some are becoming Elysium.

It is unfortunately the inequality between the have and have-nots that destroys democracies. There are few democracies in worlds of scarcity. Abundance is a necessary condition, however, it does not guarantee it.

That's because abundance does not necessarily lead to greater transparency. It only leads to greater mobility and individuality.  Left to its natural evolution, it leads to greater diversity. But nipped in the bud, it can lead to greater control.

The biggest flaw of a Western liberal world towards authoritarian empires like Russia and China is that it assumed that abundance would lead them to democracy.  Unfortunately, it doesn't as long as those in power refuse to give their power away.

It is very dangerous for authoritarian empires to engage in wars that they cannot guarantee that they can win. Wars stress the tight control of their own citizenry. They have to fight on two fronts.  Internally and externally. We see this already in Russia.

Russia is fighting a war on multiple fronts.  The obvious one is in Ukraine.  There's also an internal one. Finally, there are other borders that have a history of conflict with Russia. It's made worse by their technology dependency and deteriorating demographics.

Also, it's in everyone's interest to see Russia break up into multiple new states. It's only the citizenry west of the Urals that has an interest in keeping the status quo.  A weakened Russian army can set off a domino effect.

The problem with Russia is its lack of shared prosperity.  Societal collapse is driven by scarcity and envy.  Inequality in a world of scarcity is a very explosive mixture.  They are the fuel of internal revolutions.
